comment: Exam predictions for chemistry, derived ONLY from the five school papers 2021-2025 and their mark schemes (see the per-year notes). Every item cites the papers it is based on. Nothing here is insider knowledge — it is pattern-reading, and it is labelled as such in the app.
basis: The school's own end-of-year papers for 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, plus their mark schemes and the teachers' written commentary.
caveat: It says what the department has asked five years running and what its mark schemes reward — nothing more. Use it to decide what to revise first, never as a reason to skip a topic: papers do change, and everything on the specification is fair game.

paperShape.given: A periodic table. Nothing else — every equation must be memorised.
notes: Marks per question run 3–13; the long questions are always multi-topic (a practical, then a calculation, then an explanation).
Almost every paper opens with a short recall question (atomic structure or indicators) and ends with a calculation.
At least one full question is built on a graph you must plot or read, and at least one on a practical method you must describe.

bands.title: Nailed on
bands.note: Appeared in every single paper 2021–2025. If you revise nothing else, revise these.

items.claim: Collision theory, worded to the mark scheme
items.why: A 3-mark explanation of how concentration, temperature or surface area changes the rate. The wording is the whole test: name the change, keep the word successful, end with more collisions per unit time.

mustKnow.gist: EVERY ANSWER SAME SHAPE: (1) WHAT CHANGE, (2) SAY "SUCCESSFUL", (3) MORE HIT PER TIME. ALL THREE.
mustKnow.exact: The template for every factor: (1) what changed about the particles, (2) the word successful, (3) more collisions per unit time. All three, in that shape.

mustKnow.gist: MORE CONCENTRATED = MORE PARTICLE IN SAME SPACE = MORE HIT. NEVER SAY ENERGY HERE.
mustKnow.exact: Concentration up: more particles in the same volume → more frequent collisions. NEVER mention energy here — 2024 capped such answers at 1 of 3.

mustKnow.gist: HOTTER = PARTICLE FASTER. MORE HIT HAVE BIG ENOUGH ENERGY (BIGGER PROPORTION SUCCEED) AND MORE HIT PER TIME. TWO SEPARATE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Temperature up: particles gain kinetic energy → more collisions have energy above the ACTIVATION ENERGY (a greater proportion are successful) → and collisions are more frequent. The proportion point is its own separate mark — do not merge it with frequency.

mustKnow.gist: POWDER NOT LUMP = MORE SURFACE SHOWING = MORE HIT. SAME MASS, SO SAME AMOUNT OF PRODUCT. ONLY FASTER.
mustKnow.exact: Surface area up (powder not chips): more particles exposed → more frequent collisions. Same mass means the final amount of product is unchanged; only the speed changes.

mustKnow.gist: CATALYST = NEW PATH, AND PATH NEED LESS ENERGY. SAY BOTH HALF.
mustKnow.exact: Catalyst: provides an ALTERNATIVE PATHWAY with a LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY. Both halves — "lowers the activation energy" alone lost a mark in 2025.

mustKnow.gist: CATALYST NOT USED UP, NOT CHANGED AT END. THAT THE 2-MARK DEFINITION.
mustKnow.exact: A catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end and is not used up — that is the 2-mark definition.

mustKnow.gist: "MORE CHANCE OF HITTING" = NOTHING. WORD YOU WANT IS FREQUENCY.
mustKnow.exact: "More chance of colliding" scores nothing. The word wanted is frequency, or collisions per unit time.

practice.q: Explain, in terms of collision theory, why increasing the concentration of an acid increases the rate of reaction.
practice.a: There are more acid particles in the same volume 1; so collisions are more frequent / more collisions per unit time 1; so the rate increases 1. Any mention of kinetic energy caps this at 1 mark.

practice.q: Explain how increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
practice.a: The particles gain kinetic energy / move faster 1; more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy, so a greater PROPORTION are successful 1; and collisions are more frequent 1.

practice.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
practice.a: It provides an alternative reaction pathway 1; with a lower activation energy 1. Both halves required.

items.claim: A moles calculation: grams → moles → answer
items.why: Calculations are the single biggest slice of every paper (125 marks across five years). Expect at least one mass↔moles step, and usually a gas volume at rtp or a mass of product.

mustKnow.gist: n = MASS ÷ Mr. FLIP: MASS = n × Mr, Mr = MASS ÷ n.
mustKnow.exact: n = mass ÷ Mr. Rearranged: mass = n × Mr, and Mr = mass ÷ n.

mustKnow.gist: Mr = ADD UP ALL Ar. BRACKET MULTIPLY EVERYTHING INSIDE. Ca(OH)₂ = 40 + 2×17 = 74.
mustKnow.exact: Mr = the sum of the Ar values in the formula. Brackets multiply everything inside: Ca(OH)₂ = 40 + 2×(16+1) = 74.

mustKnow.gist: GAS AT rtp: VOLUME = n × 24 dm³, OR n × 24 000 cm³. CHECK UNIT ON ANSWER LINE FIRST.
mustKnow.exact: Gas volume at rtp: volume = n × 24 dm³, or n × 24 000 cm³. Match the unit on the answer line BEFORE calculating.

mustKnow.gist: PARTICLE COUNT = n × 6.0 × 10²³.
mustKnow.exact: Particles: number = n × 6.0 × 10²³.

mustKnow.gist: MASS QUESTION: (1) MOLE OF WHAT YOU KNOW, (2) USE EQUATION RATIO, (3) TURN INTO WHAT THEY ASK.
mustKnow.exact: Reacting-mass routine: (1) moles of what you know, (2) use the balanced equation ratio, (3) convert to what is asked.

mustKnow.gist: EXCESS QUESTION: COMPARE MOLE WITH MOLE. NEVER MASS WITH MASS.
mustKnow.exact: Excess / "show that" questions: compare MOLES needed against MOLES available — never masses.

mustKnow.gist: % YIELD = REAL MASS ÷ EXPECTED MASS × 100. TURN MOLE INTO GRAM FIRST.
mustKnow.exact: % yield = actual MASS ÷ theoretical MASS × 100. Convert expected moles to grams first — 2025 rejected actual ÷ moles.

mustKnow.gist: EMPIRICAL: DIVIDE BY Ar (NOT ATOMIC NUMBER), DIVIDE BY SMALLEST, THEN SCALE UP. 1 : 1.33 → 3 : 4.
mustKnow.exact: Empirical formula: divide each mass or % by the Ar (never the atomic number), divide by the smallest, then multiply up if you get 1 : 1.33 → 3 : 4.

mustKnow.gist: ALWAYS SHOW THE MOLE STEP. NO WORKING + WRONG ANSWER = ZERO. WORKING SAVE LATER MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Show the moles step. A wrong answer with no working scores zero; with working, error carried forward saves the later marks.

practice.q: Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced by completely decomposing 10.5 g of NaHCO₃. [2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂; Mr NaHCO₃ = 84, CO₂ = 44]
practice.a: n(NaHCO₃) = 10.5 ÷ 84 = 0.125 mol, and the 2:1 ratio gives n(CO₂) = 0.0625 mol 1; mass = 0.0625 × 44 = 2.75 g 1.

practice.q: 6.4 × 10⁶ g of sulfur burns to SO₂. Calculate the volume of gas at rtp, in standard form. [Ar S = 32; molar volume 24 dm³]
practice.a: n = 6.4 × 10⁶ ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁵ mol 1; volume = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 24 = 4 800 000 dm³ 1; = 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³ 1 — the last mark is purely for standard form.

practice.q: A compound is 90.7% lead and 9.3% oxygen. Show that its empirical formula is Pb₃O₄. [Ar Pb = 207, O = 16]
practice.a: 90.7 ÷ 207 = 0.438 1; 9.3 ÷ 16 = 0.581 1; divide by the smaller: 1 : 1.33 1; × 3 → 3 : 4 → Pb₃O₄ 1.

items.claim: Electrolysis: predict the products and write a half-equation
items.why: Every year. Know the reactivity rule for the cathode, halide-or-oxygen for the anode, and write half-equations with the electrons on the correct side.

mustKnow.gist: CATHODE = MINUS, PULL PLUS ION, ION TAKE ELECTRON = REDUCTION. ANODE = PLUS, ION GIVE ELECTRON = OXIDATION.
mustKnow.exact: Cathode is negative, attracts positive ions (cations), which gain electrons = REDUCTION. Anode is positive, attracts anions, which lose electrons = OXIDATION.

mustKnow.gist: THE ION TAKE OR GIVE ELECTRON. SAY "MAGNESIUM ION", NOT "MAGNESIUM".
mustKnow.exact: It is the ION that gains or loses electrons. 2023: "the magnesium ION gains electrons, not the magnesium!!"

mustKnow.gist: CATHODE IN SOLUTION: WHICHEVER LESS REACTIVE, METAL OR HYDROGEN. COPPER AND SILVER COME OUT. SODIUM, POTASSIUM, MAGNESIUM STAY IN — HYDROGEN COME OUT INSTEAD.
mustKnow.exact: Cathode product in solution: the LESS REACTIVE of the metal and hydrogen. Copper and silver deposit; sodium, potassium and magnesium stay in solution and HYDROGEN forms instead.

mustKnow.gist: ANODE: HALIDE THERE → HALOGEN (Cl₂, Br₂). NO HALIDE → OXYGEN FROM WATER.
mustKnow.exact: Anode product: a halide present → the halogen (Cl₂, Br₂). No halide (sulfate, nitrate) → OXYGEN from water.

mustKnow.gist: LEARN: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu · Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na · 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ · 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ · 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ · 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
mustKnow.exact: Half-equations: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu · Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na · 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ · 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ · 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ · 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

mustKnow.gist: HALOGEN COME IN PAIR: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Cl⁺ AND Cl₃ NOT REAL.
mustKnow.exact: Halogens are diatomic: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Cl⁺ and Cl₃ are invented chemistry.

mustKnow.gist: OXYGEN EQUATION START FROM WATER. NO O²⁻ ION IN SOLUTION.
mustKnow.exact: The oxygen half-equation starts from water — there are no O²⁻ ions in a solution. 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ was the year group’s favourite wrong answer in 2023.

mustKnow.gist: SOLID IONIC NOT CONDUCT BECAUSE ION STUCK IN LATTICE. NEVER SAY ELECTRON.
mustKnow.exact: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because the ions are fixed in the lattice — never say electrons.

mustKnow.gist: NaCl SOLUTION: H⁺ TAKEN AT CATHODE, OH⁻ LEFT BEHIND. GO ALKALINE. INDICATOR TURN BLUE/PURPLE.
mustKnow.exact: Electrolysing NaCl(aq): H⁺ is removed at the cathode leaving OH⁻, so the solution there turns alkaline and universal indicator goes blue/purple.

mustKnow.gist: GAS TEST: LIT SPLINT POP = HYDROGEN · GLOWING SPLINT RELIGHT = OXYGEN · LITMUS BLEACH = CHLORINE · LIMEWATER MILKY = CO₂.
mustKnow.exact: Gas tests: LIT splint squeaky pop = hydrogen · GLOWING splint relights = oxygen · damp litmus bleached = chlorine · limewater milky = CO₂.

practice.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. Write the anode half-equation and explain why it is oxidation.
practice.a: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ 1; oxidation because the bromide ions lose electrons 1. "Bromine loses electrons" is rejected.

practice.q: Explain why hydrogen, not sodium, forms at the cathode when sodium chloride SOLUTION is electrolysed.
practice.a: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so the hydrogen ions are discharged instead 1.

practice.q: Universal indicator is added near the negative electrode during electrolysis of NaCl(aq). State the colour and name the ion responsible.
practice.a: Blue/purple 1; hydroxide ions, OH⁻, left behind as H⁺ is discharged 1.

practice.q: Complete the anode half-equation for dilute sulfuric acid: ......H₂O → ......H⁺ + ......O₂ + ......e⁻
practice.a: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ 1.

items.claim: Describe a method to make a pure, dry salt
items.why: The department's favourite long-answer. Which of the three methods you pick is the real question — check the solubility rules before writing a word.

mustKnow.gist: CHECK SOLUBILITY RULE FIRST. THAT TELL YOU WHICH OF THREE METHOD TO WRITE.
mustKnow.exact: Check the solubility rules for the salt you want FIRST — that decides which of the three methods you write.

mustKnow.gist: RULE: SODIUM, POTASSIUM, AMMONIUM ALL DISSOLVE · NITRATE ALL DISSOLVE · CHLORIDE YES EXCEPT SILVER AND LEAD · SULFATE YES EXCEPT BARIUM, CALCIUM, LEAD · CARBONATE NO (EXCEPT Na/K/NH₄) · HYDROXIDE NO (EXCEPT Na/K).
mustKnow.exact: Rules: all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts soluble · all nitrates soluble · chlorides soluble EXCEPT silver and lead(II) · sulfates soluble EXCEPT barium, calcium, lead(II) · carbonates insoluble except Na/K/NH₄ · hydroxides insoluble except Na/K (Ca slightly).

mustKnow.gist: METHOD 1, SALT DISSOLVE + SOLID NOT: ADD SOLID TILL EXTRA LEFT · FILTER EXTRA OUT · HEAT TILL CRYSTAL START · COOL · POUR LIQUID OFF · DRY (SAY HOW).
mustKnow.exact: Method 1 — soluble salt + insoluble solid: add solid until in EXCESS (so all the acid reacts) · FILTER off the excess · heat the filtrate to the CRYSTALLISATION POINT · cool and crystallise · pour off the liquid · DRY with a named method.

mustKnow.gist: METHOD 2, BOTH DISSOLVE: TITRATE WITH INDICATOR TO GET VOLUME · DO AGAIN SAME VOLUME NO INDICATOR · THEN CRYSTALLISE.
mustKnow.exact: Method 2 — soluble salt, both reactants soluble: titrate with indicator to find the volumes · repeat with the same volumes WITHOUT indicator · crystallise as above.

mustKnow.gist: METHOD 3, SALT NOT DISSOLVE: MIX TWO SOLUTION · FILTER · WASH THE SOLID WITH DISTILLED WATER · DRY GENTLE.
mustKnow.exact: Method 3 — insoluble salt: MIX TWO SOLUTIONS · filter · WASH THE RESIDUE with distilled water · dry gently (filter paper or warm oven, never a Bunsen).

mustKnow.gist: NEVER BOIL DRY. WATER OF CRYSTALLISATION GO AWAY. CAP YOU AT 1 MARK.
mustKnow.exact: NEVER heat to dryness for hydrated crystals — caps the answer at 1 mark, because the water of crystallisation is driven off.

mustKnow.gist: "LEAVE TO DRY" NOT ENOUGH. SAY HOW: FILTER PAPER, WARM PLACE, WARM OVEN.
mustKnow.exact: "Leave the crystals to dry" without a method loses the final mark. Name it: filter paper, warm place, warm oven.

mustKnow.gist: IN PRECIPITATION THE SALT YOU WANT IS THE SOLID LEFT BEHIND, NOT THE LIQUID.
mustKnow.exact: In a precipitation the salt you want is the residue, not the filtrate.

mustKnow.gist: CANNOT FILTER OUT A SALT THAT DISSOLVE. SODIUM SALT ALWAYS DISSOLVE.
mustKnow.exact: You cannot filter out a soluble salt — sodium salts are always soluble.

practice.q: Describe how to obtain pure, dry crystals of zinc nitrate from zinc powder and dilute nitric acid.
practice.a: Add excess zinc so all the acid reacts, then FILTER off the excess 1; heat the filtrate to the crystallisation point 1; leave to cool and crystallise 1; pour off or filter the remaining liquid 1; dry with filter paper or in a warm oven 1.

practice.q: Describe how to obtain pure, dry lead(II) bromide from lead(II) nitrate solution and sodium bromide solution.
practice.a: Mix the two SOLUTIONS 1; filter 1; wash the RESIDUE with distilled water 1; dry with filter paper or in a warm oven, not by direct heating 1.

practice.q: A student plans to make hydrated magnesium sulfate using nitric acid and "a solution of magnesium carbonate", then boiling off all the water. Identify the three mistakes.
practice.a: Wrong acid — a sulfate needs SULFURIC acid 1; magnesium carbonate is INSOLUBLE, so there is no solution of it — add the solid 1; boiling to dryness destroys the hydrated crystals — heat to the crystallisation point and cool 1.

items.claim: Structure and bonding explaining a physical property
items.why: Melting point, conductivity or hardness explained from the structure. Choose the right model first: giant ionic, giant covalent, simple molecular or metallic.

mustKnow.gist: PICK THE STRUCTURE FIRST: GIANT IONIC, GIANT COVALENT, SIMPLE MOLECULAR, GIANT METALLIC. WRONG ONE = ZERO, NOT HALF.
mustKnow.exact: Decide the structure first: giant ionic, giant covalent, simple molecular, or giant metallic. The wrong model scores zero, not partial credit.

mustKnow.gist: GIANT IONIC HIGH MELT (3 MARK): GIANT LATTICE · STRONG PULL BETWEEN OPPOSITE ION · LOTS OF ENERGY TO BREAK. SAY MOLECULE OR COVALENT HERE = ZERO.
mustKnow.exact: Giant ionic high melting point (3 marks): giant ionic lattice · STRONG attraction between OPPOSITELY CHARGED IONS · lots of energy to overcome. Any covalent/molecule/IMF language = 0 marks (2025).

mustKnow.gist: SIMPLE MOLECULAR LOW BOIL (2 MARK): WEAK FORCE BETWEEN MOLECULE · LITTLE ENERGY TO BREAK. SAY COVALENT BOND HERE = ZERO.
mustKnow.exact: Simple molecular low boiling point (2 marks): WEAK intermolecular forces BETWEEN MOLECULES · little energy to overcome them. Any reference to breaking covalent bonds = 0/2 (2021).

mustKnow.gist: BIGGER MOLECULE = STRONGER FORCE BETWEEN THEM = HIGHER BOILING. BETWEEN MOLECULE, NOT BETWEEN ATOM.
mustKnow.exact: Bigger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point. Forces between molecules, never between atoms.

mustKnow.gist: GIANT COVALENT (DIAMOND, GRAPHITE, SiO₂): MELTING DO BREAK COVALENT BOND. ONLY PLACE THAT TRUE.
mustKnow.exact: Giant covalent (diamond, graphite, SiO₂): melting BREAKS COVALENT BONDS — the one place that phrase is correct.

mustKnow.gist: C₆₀ IS SIMPLE MOLECULAR EVEN WITH 60 ATOM, SO MELT WAY BELOW GRAPHITE. NEVER PUT WEAK FORCE IN GRAPHITE.
mustKnow.exact: C₆₀ fullerene is simple molecular despite 60 atoms, so it melts far below graphite. Never put intermolecular forces in graphite.

mustKnow.gist: COVALENT BOND = SHARED PAIR PULLED BY NUCLEI OF BOTH ATOM. SAY BOTH — "NUCLEUS" LOSE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: A covalent bond = a SHARED PAIR of electrons attracted to the nuclei of BOTH atoms. Plural — "nucleus" loses the mark.

mustKnow.gist: METALLIC = PLUS ION IN SEA OF DELOCALISED ELECTRON. NOT PROTON. BENDY BECAUSE LAYER OF ION SLIDE.
mustKnow.exact: Metallic: positive IONS in a sea of DELOCALISED ELECTRONS ("protons" is rejected). Malleable because LAYERS OF IONS SLIDE over one another.

mustKnow.gist: CONDUCT: METAL AND GRAPHITE BY ELECTRON · IONIC ONLY WHEN MELTED OR DISSOLVED, BECAUSE ION CAN MOVE · SIMPLE MOLECULAR NEVER.
mustKnow.exact: Conduction: metals and graphite via delocalised electrons · ionic only when MOLTEN or DISSOLVED because then the IONS move · simple molecular never.

mustKnow.gist: IONIC STORY MUST COUNT ELECTRON: "MAGNESIUM LOSE TWO, OXYGEN GAIN TWO".
mustKnow.exact: Ionic bonding stories must COUNT the electrons: "magnesium loses TWO electrons, oxygen gains TWO".

practice.q: Explain why magnesium oxide has a very high melting point.
practice.a: Giant ionic structure/lattice 1; strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions 1; a lot of energy is needed to overcome them 1. Covalent/molecule/IMF language scores 0.

practice.q: The bonding in a hydrogen molecule is strong, yet hydrogen boils at −253 °C. Explain why.
practice.a: There are only weak intermolecular forces between the molecules 1; so little energy is needed to overcome them and separate the molecules 1. Bond-breaking answers score 0/2.

practice.q: Explain why C₆₀ fullerene has a much lower melting point than graphite.
practice.a: Graphite is giant covalent 1; melting graphite breaks covalent bonds 1; C₆₀ is simple molecular 1; melting C₆₀ only overcomes intermolecular forces, needing far less energy 1.

practice.q: Explain why magnesium is malleable.
practice.a: The positive ions are arranged in layers 1; the layers slide over one another while the metallic bonding is maintained 1. No intermolecular forces here.

bands.title: Very likely — repeated almost verbatim
bands.note: These have been re-set with the same wording and the same mark scheme. Learn the mark points, not just the topic.

items.claim: The fractional distillation four-marker
items.why: Three years running, identical mark scheme: heated/vaporised · vapours RISE · hotter at the bottom · each condenses where the column is cooler than its boiling point. The two marks that go missing are 'rise' and tying condensation to the boiling point.

mustKnow.gist: FOUR MARK IN ORDER: (1) HEAT IT TO VAPOUR · (2) VAPOUR RISE · (3) BOTTOM HOTTER THAN TOP · (4) EACH VAPOUR RISE TILL IT CONDENSE, WHERE COLUMN COLDER THAN ITS BOILING POINT.
mustKnow.exact: The four mark points in order: (1) the oil is heated / vaporised · (2) the vapours RISE up the column · (3) the column is hotter at the bottom · (4) each vapour rises until it condenses, where the column temperature falls BELOW ITS BOILING POINT.

mustKnow.gist: TWO MARK ALWAYS LOST: THE WORD "RISE", AND TYING CONDENSING TO BOILING POINT. "TURN TO LIQUID" NOT ENOUGH.
mustKnow.exact: The two marks that go missing every year are "rise" and tying condensation to the BOILING POINT. "Turns to liquid" alone is not enough.

mustKnow.gist: FRACTIONATING COLUMN = THE KIT. FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION = THE PROCESS. READ WHICH THEY ASK.
mustKnow.exact: Fractionating column = the equipment; fractional distillation = the process. 2022 asked for the equipment and ignored the process name.

mustKnow.gist: TOP TO BOTTOM: REFINERY GAS · PETROL · KEROSENE · DIESEL · FUEL OIL · BITUMEN.
mustKnow.exact: Fractions top to bottom: refinery gases · gasoline (petrol) · kerosene (jet fuel) · diesel · fuel oil (ships, power stations) · bitumen (roads).

mustKnow.gist: GOING DOWN: LONGER · HIGHER BOILING · DARKER · THICKER · HARDER TO BURN.
mustKnow.exact: Going DOWN: longer molecules · higher boiling point · darker · more viscous · less flammable.

mustKnow.gist: FRACTION = HYDROCARBON WITH SIMILAR BOILING POINT. CRUDE OIL = MIXTURE. HYDROCARBON = HYDROGEN AND CARBON ONLY.
mustKnow.exact: A fraction = hydrocarbons with SIMILAR BOILING POINTS. Crude oil is a MIXTURE of hydrocarbons — compounds of hydrogen and carbon ONLY.

practice.q: Describe how crude oil is separated into fractions in a fractionating column.
practice.a: The crude oil is heated/vaporised 1; the vapours rise up the column 1; the column is hotter at the bottom than the top 1; each vapour rises until it condenses, where the column temperature is below its boiling point 1.

practice.q: Explain why a hydrocarbon in fuel oil has a higher boiling point than one in refinery gases.
practice.a: Fuel oil molecules have longer chains 1; stronger intermolecular forces between the molecules 1; more energy needed to overcome them 1.

items.claim: "Explain the role of carbon" — reducing agent, removes oxygen
items.why: Asked in consecutive years with the same two mark points, and fluffed both times. Say reducing agent, then say it REMOVES oxygen from the fully named compound.
items.evidence: 2024 Q8c and 2025 Q6c — the same question twice

mustKnow.gist: TWO MARK, TWO FACT: (1) CARBON IS THE REDUCING AGENT · (2) IT REMOVE OXYGEN FROM [FULL NAME OF COMPOUND].
mustKnow.exact: Two marks, two facts: (1) carbon is the reducing agent · (2) it REMOVES OXYGEN FROM [the full name of the compound].

mustKnow.gist: NO MARK FOR "REACT WITH OXYGEN" OR "DISPLACE OXYGEN". WORD IS REMOVE.
mustKnow.exact: Rejected: "reacts with the oxygen", "displaces the oxygen". The word wanted is REMOVES (or the compound LOSES oxygen).

mustKnow.gist: NAME THE WHOLE COMPOUND — CALCIUM PHOSPHATE, IRON(III) OXIDE. NOT JUST THE METAL.
mustKnow.exact: Name the WHOLE compound — calcium phosphate, copper(II) oxide, iron(III) oxide — not just the metal.

mustKnow.gist: REDUCTION = LOSE OXYGEN. OXIDATION = GAIN OXYGEN. REDUCING AGENT GET OXIDISED ITSELF.
mustKnow.exact: REDUCTION = loss of oxygen. OXIDATION = gain of oxygen. The reducing agent is itself oxidised.

mustKnow.gist: REDOX ANSWER NAME BOTH: "ALUMINIUM OXIDISED, GAIN OXYGEN; IRON(III) OXIDE REDUCED, LOSE OXYGEN". "IRON IS REDUCED" LOSE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: In a redox explanation name BOTH species and BOTH directions: "aluminium is oxidised because it gains oxygen; iron(III) OXIDE is reduced because it loses oxygen". "Iron is reduced" loses the mark.

mustKnow.gist: "OXIDATION AND REDUCTION HAPPEN TOGETHER" ALONE = NOTHING.
mustKnow.exact: "Oxidation and reduction happen at the same time" on its own scores nothing.

practice.q: In Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO, explain the role of carbon.
practice.a: Carbon is the reducing agent 1; it removes the oxygen from the calcium phosphate 1.

practice.q: Explain why 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe is a redox reaction.
practice.a: Aluminium is oxidised because it gains oxygen 1; iron(III) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen 1. "Iron is reduced" loses the mark.

items.claim: Sulfur → SO₂ gas volume, answer in standard form
items.why: Re-used word for word between two papers, down to the 6.4 tonnes. Third mark is purely for standard form.

mustKnow.gist: THREE MARK: (1) MOLE = MASS ÷ 32 · (2) × 24 FOR dm³ · (3) WRITE IT IN STANDARD FORM.
mustKnow.exact: Three marks: (1) moles of sulfur = mass ÷ 32 · (2) × 24 for the volume in dm³ · (3) the answer in standard form.

mustKnow.gist: 6.4 TONNE = 6.4 × 10⁶ g. TONNE TO GRAM IS × 10⁶.
mustKnow.exact: 6.4 tonnes = 6.4 × 10⁶ g. Tonnes → grams is × 10⁶.

mustKnow.gist: WRITE 4 800 000 AND YOU GET 2 OF 3. THIRD MARK ONLY FOR THE NOTATION.
mustKnow.exact: Writing 4 800 000 without standard form scores 2 of 3 — the third mark is purely for the notation.

mustKnow.gist: S : SO₂ IS 1 : 1, SO MOLE GO STRAIGHT ACROSS.
mustKnow.exact: The S : SO₂ ratio is 1 : 1, so the moles carry straight across.

mustKnow.gist: THIS EXACT SUM, SAME NUMBER, CAME UP ON TWO PAPERS.
mustKnow.exact: This exact question, with the same numbers, appeared on two different papers.

practice.q: 3.2 tonnes of sulfur is burned to SO₂. Calculate the volume of gas at rtp, in standard form. [Ar S = 32; molar volume 24 dm³]
practice.a: n = 3.2 × 10⁶ ÷ 32 = 1.0 × 10⁵ mol 1; volume = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 24 = 2 400 000 dm³ 1; = 2.4 × 10⁶ dm³ 1.

items.claim: Read a solubility curve, then find the mass that crystallises on cooling
items.why: Four of five years, and growing (4 marks in 2022–23, 10 marks in 2024 and 2025). Two readings and a subtraction — with the construction lines drawn on the graph.

mustKnow.gist: SOLUBILITY = GRAM THAT FILL UP 100 g OF WATER AT A GIVEN TEMPERATURE. ALWAYS SAY THE TEMPERATURE.
mustKnow.exact: Solubility = grams of solute saturating 100 g of water at a stated temperature. The temperature must always be given.

mustKnow.gist: MASS THAT COME OUT ON COOLING = HOT VALUE − COLD VALUE, THEN SCALE TO THE WATER USED.
mustKnow.exact: Mass crystallising on cooling = (solubility hot) − (solubility cold), then scaled to the water actually used.

mustKnow.gist: SCALE STRAIGHT: 250 g OF WATER = × 2.5. TABLE PER 25 cm³ = × 4. 1 cm³ WATER WEIGH 1 g.
mustKnow.exact: Scale linearly: per 250 g of water × 2.5. If the table is per 25 cm³, × 4 — 1 cm³ of water has a mass of 1 g.

mustKnow.gist: WHERE TWO CURVE CROSS, BOTH SALT SAME SOLUBILITY. DROP A LINE DOWN AND SHOW IT.
mustKnow.exact: Where two curves cross, the salts have equal solubility. Drop a vertical line and SHOW it.

mustKnow.gist: SHOW YOUR LINES FOR EVERY VALUE YOU READ. LINES CARRY THEIR OWN MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Show your construction lines for every value read off — they carry their own mark, penalised in 2023, 2024 and 2025.

mustKnow.gist: READ THE CURVE THEY NAME. EASY TO READ THE WRONG ONE.
mustKnow.exact: Read the curve the question names. 2023: several read the wrong curve entirely.

mustKnow.gist: SATURATED = NO MORE WILL DISSOLVE AT THAT TEMPERATURE.
mustKnow.exact: A saturated solution = no more solute will dissolve AT THAT TEMPERATURE.

mustKnow.gist: NEAR 100 °C LESS ACCURATE BECAUSE WATER EVAPORATE.
mustKnow.exact: Values near 100 °C are less accurate because water EVAPORATES during the experiment.

practice.q: Solubility is 45 g/100 g at 60 °C and 13 g/100 g at 10 °C. A saturated solution in 100 g of water cools from 60 to 10 °C. Calculate the mass that crystallises.
practice.a: Read both values, 45 and 13 1; 45 − 13 = 32 g 1. Show the construction lines.

practice.q: A table gives 24 g of salt dissolving in 25 cm³ of water. Calculate the solubility in g per 100 g of water.
practice.a: 1 cm³ of water = 1 g, so 25 cm³ = 25 g of water 1; × 4 → 96 g per 100 g 1.

items.claim: Water of crystallisation: find x in a hydrated salt
items.why: Three appearances with the same shape — masses before and after heating to constant mass, then a mole ratio. Also expect "why is x too low?" (not heated long enough).

mustKnow.gist: HEAT CRYSTAL TILL MASS STOP CHANGING. WHAT LEFT = DRY SALT. WHAT LOST = WATER.
mustKnow.exact: The method: heat the hydrated crystals to constant mass. The mass remaining = anhydrous salt; the mass LOST = water.

mustKnow.gist: THEN: MOLE OF SALT = MASS ÷ Mr · MOLE OF WATER = MASS ÷ 18 · DIVIDE BOTH BY SMALLER → 1 : x.
mustKnow.exact: Then: moles of salt = mass ÷ Mr · moles of water = mass ÷ 18 · divide both by the smaller → the ratio 1 : x.

mustKnow.gist: "CONSTANT MASS" = HEAT, COOL, WEIGH, AGAIN AND AGAIN TILL MASS STOP MOVING. THAT THE PROOF.
mustKnow.exact: Heating to constant mass = repeatedly heating, cooling and reweighing until the mass stops changing — the proof all the water has gone.

mustKnow.gist: x TOO SMALL? NOT HEATED LONG ENOUGH, WATER STILL IN. FIX: HEAT AGAIN TO CONSTANT MASS.
mustKnow.exact: If x comes out too low: not heated long enough, so not all the water was driven off. Fix: reheat to constant mass.

mustKnow.gist: HYDRATED = HAS WATER OF CRYSTALLISATION, WRITTEN ·xH₂O. WITHOUT IT = ANHYDROUS.
mustKnow.exact: "Hydrated" means it contains WATER OF CRYSTALLISATION, written ·xH₂O. Without it: anhydrous.

mustKnow.gist: Mr OF WATER = 18. MOST USED NUMBER HERE.
mustKnow.exact: Mr of water is 18 — the most-used number in this calculation.

practice.q: Heating Na₂CO₃·xH₂O gives 3.18 g of Na₂CO₃ and loses 3.78 g of water. Show that x = 7. [Mr Na₂CO₃ = 106]
practice.a: n(Na₂CO₃) = 3.18 ÷ 106 = 0.03 1; n(H₂O) = 3.78 ÷ 18 = 0.21 1; 0.21 ÷ 0.03 = 7, so x = 7 1.

practice.q: A student’s value of x is lower than the true value. Explain why, and how to improve the method.
practice.a: The crystals were not heated long enough, so not all the water of crystallisation was removed 1; reheat, cool and reweigh until the mass is constant 1.

items.claim: A dot-and-cross diagram
items.why: Four years out of five, a different molecule each time (HCl, N₂, NH₃, H₂O₂). Two marks: the bonding pairs, then everything else exactly right.

mustKnow.gist: TWO MARK: (1) RIGHT NUMBER OF BONDING PAIR, (2) EVERYTHING ELSE RIGHT — THE LONE PAIR.
mustKnow.exact: Two marks: (1) the correct bonding pairs, (2) everything else correct — the lone pairs.

mustKnow.gist: OUTER ELECTRON ONLY. DOT OR CROSS, EITHER FINE.
mustKnow.exact: Show OUTER electrons only unless told otherwise. Any mix of dots and crosses is accepted.

mustKnow.gist: COUNT OUTER ELECTRON, GIVE EVERY ATOM FULL SHELL. HYDROGEN 2, REST 8.
mustKnow.exact: Count each atom’s outer electrons and give every atom a full shell (2 for hydrogen, 8 for the rest).

mustKnow.gist: ONES THAT COME UP: HCl 1 SHARED + 3 LONE ON Cl · NH₃ 3 BONDING + 1 LONE ON N · H₂O₂ 3 BONDING + 2 LONE ON EACH O · N₂ TRIPLE BOND, 6 SHARED, 1 LONE EACH.
mustKnow.exact: The ones that have come up: HCl — one shared pair, three lone pairs on Cl · NH₃ — three bonding pairs, one lone pair on N · H₂O₂ (H–O–O–H) — three bonding pairs, two lone pairs on each O · N₂ — a TRIPLE bond, SIX shared electrons, one lone pair on each N.

mustKnow.gist: WATER = 2 BONDING + 2 LONE ON OXYGEN. METHANE = 4 BONDING, NO LONE.
mustKnow.exact: Water H₂O — two bonding pairs, two lone pairs on oxygen. Methane CH₄ — four bonding pairs, no lone pairs.

mustKnow.gist: IONIC ONE: SHOW THE MOVE AND THE CHARGE. Na⁺ [2.8] AND Cl⁻ [2.8.8] IN SQUARE BRACKET.
mustKnow.exact: For an IONIC dot-and-cross, show the transfer and the charges: Na⁺ [2.8] and Cl⁻ [2.8.8] in square brackets.

practice.q: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for ammonia, NH₃, showing outer electrons only.
practice.a: Three N–H bonding pairs 1; one lone pair on the nitrogen and the rest fully correct 1.

practice.q: How many electrons are shared in N₂, and what does each atom keep?
practice.a: Six electrons shared — a triple bond 1; each nitrogen keeps one lone pair 1.

items.claim: Alkanes: isomers, displayed formulae, and CH₄ + Br₂ substitution
items.why: The organic block is worth ~14 marks a year. Expect to define isomers (say MOLECULAR formula), draw displayed formulae with every C–H bond, and name substitution with UV light.

mustKnow.gist: ISOMER = SAME MOLECULAR FORMULA, DIFFERENT SHAPE DRAWN. SAY "MOLECULAR", NOT "CHEMICAL".
mustKnow.exact: Isomers = same MOLECULAR formula, different structural/displayed formulae. "Same chemical formula" lost the mark in 2023.

mustKnow.gist: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. METHANE CH₄ · ETHANE C₂H₆ · PROPANE C₃H₈ · BUTANE C₄H₁₀ · PENTANE C₅H₁₂.
mustKnow.exact: General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Methane CH₄ · ethane C₂H₆ · propane C₃H₈ · butane C₄H₁₀ · pentane C₅H₁₂.

mustKnow.gist: DISPLAYED = DRAW EVERY ATOM AND EVERY BOND, INCLUDING ALL C–H. A LUMP LIKE –CH₃ = NO MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Displayed formula = every atom and every bond drawn, including all C–H bonds. A –CH₃ written as a lump is rejected.

mustKnow.gist: EVERY CARBON NEED EXACTLY FOUR BOND. COUNT BEFORE YOU MOVE ON.
mustKnow.exact: Every carbon must have exactly FOUR bonds. Count them before moving on.

mustKnow.gist: C₄H₁₀ HAS TWO: BUTANE, METHYLPROPANE. C₅H₁₂ HAS THREE: PENTANE, 2-METHYLBUTANE, 2,2-DIMETHYLPROPANE.
mustKnow.exact: C₄H₁₀ has two isomers: butane and methylpropane. C₅H₁₂ has three: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane.

mustKnow.gist: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr, NEED UV LIGHT. TYPE = SUBSTITUTION. NOT ADDITION, NOT DISPLACEMENT.
mustKnow.exact: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr, requiring ultraviolet light. The type is substitution — not displacement, addition or reduction.

mustKnow.gist: WRITE HBr, NOT HBR. WRITE PROPANE, NOT "TRIANE".
mustKnow.exact: Case matters: HBr, not HBR. Spelling matters: propane, not "triane".

mustKnow.gist: ALKANE ARE SATURATED — ONLY SINGLE C–C BOND — SO THEY SWAP ATOM, NOT ADD.
mustKnow.exact: Alkanes are SATURATED — only single C–C bonds — which is why they substitute rather than add.

mustKnow.gist: FULL BURN GIVE CO₂ AND WATER. NOT HYDROGEN. BAD BURN GIVE CARBON MONOXIDE — POISON, IT CUT HOW MUCH OXYGEN BLOOD CAN CARRY.
mustKnow.exact: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and WATER ("hydrogen" is the classic error). Incomplete gives carbon monoxide, poisonous because it reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen.

practice.q: State what is meant by isomers, then name the two isomers of C₄H₁₀.
practice.a: Same MOLECULAR formula 1; different structural/displayed formulae 1; butane and methylpropane 1.

practice.q: Methane reacts with bromine. Give both products, the condition needed, and the reaction type.
practice.a: CH₃Br 1 and HBr 1; ultraviolet light 1; substitution 1.

practice.q: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethane, C₂H₆.
practice.a: Products CO₂ and H₂O 1; 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O 1.

items.claim: Balance an equation and add state symbols
items.why: Woven through every paper rather than asked alone. The marks are lost to missing balancing numbers and to writing a dissolved salt as (s).

mustKnow.gist: BALANCE WITH BIG NUMBER IN FRONT ONLY. NEVER CHANGE THE LITTLE NUMBER — THAT MAKE A DIFFERENT SUBSTANCE.
mustKnow.exact: Balance with the big numbers in front only. Never change a subscript — that invents a different substance.

mustKnow.gist: WRITE FORMULA RIGHT FIRST, THEN BALANCE, THEN COUNT EVERY ELEMENT AGAIN.
mustKnow.exact: Write correct formulae FIRST (from the ion charges), then balance, then RECOUNT every element.

mustKnow.gist: MARK: FORMULA 1, BALANCING 1. MOST COMMON LOSS = FORGOT THE BIG NUMBER.
mustKnow.exact: Marks are usually: formulae 1, balancing 1. 2024: "many got close but did not include balancing numbers".

mustKnow.gist: STATE SYMBOL: (s) SOLID · (l) PURE LIQUID · (g) GAS · (aq) DISSOLVED IN WATER.
mustKnow.exact: State symbols: (s) solid · (l) pure liquid · (g) gas · (aq) DISSOLVED IN WATER.

mustKnow.gist: WATER IS (l), NEVER (aq). SALT MADE IN SOLUTION IS (aq). SOLID THAT DROP OUT IS (s).
mustKnow.exact: Water is (l), never (aq). A soluble salt formed in solution is (aq) — 2024: many wrongly wrote zinc nitrate as (s) or (l). A precipitate is (s).

mustKnow.gist: CHARGE: GROUP 1/2/3 → +1/+2/+3 · GROUP 5/6/7 → −3/−2/−1 · Ag⁺ Zn²⁺ Cu²⁺ Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ Pb²⁺ · H⁺ OH⁻ NH₄⁺ NO₃⁻ CO₃²⁻ SO₄²⁻.
mustKnow.exact: Ion charges: Groups 1/2/3 → +1/+2/+3 · Groups 5/6/7 → −3/−2/−1 · Ag⁺ Zn²⁺ Cu²⁺ Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ Pb²⁺ · H⁺ OH⁻ NH₄⁺ NO₃⁻ CO₃²⁻ SO₄²⁻.

mustKnow.gist: BRACKET WHEN YOU MULTIPLY A GROUP: (NH₄)₂SO₄, Ca(NO₃)₂, Al₂(SO₄)₃.
mustKnow.exact: Brackets when a molecular ion is multiplied: (NH₄)₂SO₄, Ca(NO₃)₂, Al₂(SO₄)₃.

mustKnow.gist: THESE COME IN PAIR: H₂ N₂ O₂ F₂ Cl₂ Br₂ I₂.
mustKnow.exact: Diatomic elements: H₂ N₂ O₂ F₂ Cl₂ Br₂ I₂.

mustKnow.gist: LEARN THESE: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO · 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ · 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂ · Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO.
mustKnow.exact: Set pieces: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO · 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ · 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂ · Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO · Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃.

practice.q: Add state symbols: CaCO₃(...) + 2HCl(...) → CaCl₂(...) + H₂O(...) + CO₂(...)
practice.a: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) 1 → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) 1.

practice.q: Balance: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + ......C → Ca₃P₂ + ......CO
practice.a: 8 and 8 1 — the bracket holds 2 × 4 = 8 oxygens, each leaving in one CO.

practice.q: Give the formula of ammonium sulfate and the equation for its formation from ammonia and sulfuric acid.
practice.a: (NH₄)₂SO₄ 1; 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄ 1.

bands.title: Due a return
bands.note: On the school's own checklist but absent or rare in recent papers — the classic setter's move is to bring one of these back.

items.claim: Cracking — conditions, why it is done, and an equation
items.why: It is on the department's topic checklist (spec 4.17–4.18) but has not appeared in ANY of the five papers I have. That makes it the strongest candidate for a fresh question: silica or alumina catalyst, 600–700 °C, and supply-versus-demand as the reason.

mustKnow.gist: CRACKING = BREAK LONG ALKANE INTO SHORT ALKANE + ALKENE.
mustKnow.exact: Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes + ALKENES.

mustKnow.gist: CONDITION: SILICA OR ALUMINA CATALYST, 600–700 °C.
mustKnow.exact: Conditions: a silica or alumina catalyst at 600–700 °C.

mustKnow.gist: WHY: EVERYONE WANT PETROL, TOO MUCH LONG STUFF LEFT OVER. CRACKING MATCH SUPPLY TO DEMAND. ALKENE ALSO MAKE PLASTIC.
mustKnow.exact: Why: demand for short fractions (petrol) exceeds supply, while long fractions are in surplus — cracking matches supply to demand. The alkenes also feed plastics manufacture.

mustKnow.gist: EQUATION JUST KEEP ATOM COUNT: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. CHECK C AND H BOTH.
mustKnow.exact: A cracking equation just conserves atoms: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Check carbons and hydrogens both balance.

mustKnow.gist: ONE PRODUCT MUST BE ALKENE (CₙH₂ₙ). NOT ENOUGH HYDROGEN TO GO ROUND, SO DOUBLE BOND FORM.
mustKnow.exact: At least one product must be an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ) — hydrogens are conserved but the fragments need fewer, so a double bond forms.

mustKnow.gist: ON YOUR CHECKLIST BUT NOT IN ANY OF FIVE PAPER — SO MOST LIKELY NEW QUESTION.
mustKnow.exact: On the school checklist but absent from all five papers — which is exactly why it is the strongest candidate for a fresh question.

practice.q: Name the process converting long-chain alkanes into shorter ones, and state the conditions.
practice.a: (Catalytic) cracking 1; a silica or alumina catalyst at 600–700 °C 1.

practice.q: Complete: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + ...... and explain why cracking is carried out.
practice.a: C₄H₈ 1 (12−8 = 4 C, 26−18 = 8 H, so an alkene); demand for short fractions exceeds supply while long fractions are in surplus 1.

items.claim: Metal extraction as a full question, not a sub-part
items.why: Only three years out of five, and usually just one part buried inside another question. The reactivity series, native metals, and carbon-versus-electrolysis reasoning would make an easy stand-alone question.
items.evidence: 2021 Q10b, 2024 Q5a, 2025 (via role of carbon only)

mustKnow.gist: ORDER: POTASSIUM, SODIUM, LITHIUM, CALCIUM, MAGNESIUM, ALUMINIUM, (CARBON), ZINC, IRON, (HYDROGEN), COPPER, SILVER, GOLD.
mustKnow.exact: Reactivity series: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (CARBON), zinc, iron, (HYDROGEN), copper, silver, gold.

mustKnow.gist: ABOVE CARBON → ELECTROLYSIS OF MELTED COMPOUND (ALUMINIUM). BELOW CARBON → HEAT OXIDE WITH CARBON (IRON, ZINC, COPPER).
mustKnow.exact: Above carbon → electrolysis of the MOLTEN compound (aluminium). Below carbon → heat the oxide WITH CARBON (iron, zinc, copper).

mustKnow.gist: WHY USE CARBON WHEN YOU CAN: COKE MUCH CHEAPER THAN ELECTRIC. NOT A CHOICE — REACTIVITY DECIDE.
mustKnow.exact: Why carbon wherever possible: coke is far cheaper than electricity. Reactivity forces the expensive method; it is not a choice.

mustKnow.gist: WHY CARBON CANNOT DO THE TOP ONES: METAL MORE REACTIVE THAN CARBON, SO CARBON CANNOT TAKE ITS OXYGEN.
mustKnow.exact: Why a metal above carbon cannot use carbon: the metal is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove its oxygen.

mustKnow.gist: ORE = ROCK WITH ENOUGH METAL IN TO BE WORTH IT. NATIVE = FOUND AS PURE METAL BECAUSE VERY UNREACTIVE (GOLD).
mustKnow.exact: Ore = a rock containing enough metal compound to be worth extracting. Native = found uncombined because the metal is very UNREACTIVE (gold).

mustKnow.gist: DISPLACEMENT: STRONGER METAL KICK OUT WEAKER ONE. MAGNESIUM IN COPPER SULFATE: BLUE FADE, BROWN/PINK SOLID APPEAR.
mustKnow.exact: Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one. Zinc or magnesium in copper sulfate: the blue fades and a brown/pink solid appears.

mustKnow.gist: "NO REACTION" IS A REAL ANSWER WHEN THE METAL YOU ADD IS WEAKER.
mustKnow.exact: "No reaction" is a valid answer when the added metal is less reactive.

practice.q: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis but iron is extracted using carbon.
practice.a: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from its oxide 1; iron is below carbon so carbon can reduce its oxide 1; carbon is used wherever possible because coke is much cheaper than electricity 1.

practice.q: Magnesium is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Give two observations and explain why the reaction happens.
practice.a: The blue colour fades 1; a brown/pink solid (copper) forms on the ribbon 1; magnesium is more reactive than copper so it displaces it 1.

items.claim: Gas tests as a set
items.why: Appeared as a group for the first time in 2025 (hydrogen and oxygen with splints). Once a department starts asking these they tend to keep going — know all four: lit splint pop, glowing splint relights, limewater milky, damp litmus bleached.

mustKnow.gist: HYDROGEN: LIT SPLINT, SQUEAKY POP.
mustKnow.exact: Hydrogen: a LIT splint gives a squeaky pop.

mustKnow.gist: OXYGEN: GLOWING SPLINT RELIGHT.
mustKnow.exact: Oxygen: a GLOWING splint relights.

mustKnow.gist: CARBON DIOXIDE: LIMEWATER GO MILKY.
mustKnow.exact: Carbon dioxide: turns limewater milky/cloudy.

mustKnow.gist: CHLORINE: BLEACH DAMP LITMUS PAPER.
mustKnow.exact: Chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper.

mustKnow.gist: LIT AND GLOWING NOT THE SAME WORD. GLOWING FOR HYDROGEN = NO MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Lit and glowing are NOT interchangeable — 2024 rejected the glowing splint for hydrogen.

mustKnow.gist: OBSERVATION = WHAT YOU SEE, LIKE BUBBLES. NAMING THE GAS IS A CONCLUSION, NOT AN OBSERVATION.
mustKnow.exact: An OBSERVATION is what you see: effervescence/bubbles. Naming the gas is a conclusion and scores nothing as an observation.

practice.q: Give the test and result for hydrogen and for oxygen.
practice.a: Hydrogen: a LIT splint gives a squeaky pop 1. Oxygen: a GLOWING splint relights 1.

practice.q: A gas turns limewater milky. Identify it, and state what you would SEE when it is first produced.
practice.a: Carbon dioxide 1; effervescence / bubbles / fizzing 1 — not "carbon dioxide is given off", which is a conclusion.

items.claim: Ar from isotopic abundances
items.why: Appeared once (2023) and is a quick, self-contained three marks — exactly the kind of question that reappears after a gap.

mustKnow.gist: Ar = ADD UP (MASS × %) THEN ÷ 100. WEIGHTED AVERAGE.
mustKnow.exact: Ar = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance) ÷ 100 — a weighted mean.

mustKnow.gist: CHECK: ANSWER MUST SIT BETWEEN THE TWO MASS, CLOSER TO THE COMMON ONE.
mustKnow.exact: Sanity check: the answer must lie BETWEEN the isotope masses, nearer the more abundant one.

mustKnow.gist: GIVE 3 SIG FIG UNLESS TOLD OTHERWISE.
mustKnow.exact: Give 3 significant figures unless told otherwise.

mustKnow.gist: ISOTOPE = SAME PROTON, DIFFERENT NEUTRON. SAME ELECTRON, SO SAME CHEMISTRY.
mustKnow.exact: Isotopes = same number of protons, DIFFERENT number of neutrons. Same electron arrangement, so identical chemistry.

mustKnow.gist: ATOMIC NUMBER = PROTON. MASS NUMBER = PROTON + NEUTRON. ELECTRON WEIGH NOTHING.
mustKnow.exact: Atomic number = protons only. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Electrons weigh essentially nothing.

practice.q: Copper is 69.5% ⁶³Cu and 30.5% ⁶⁵Cu. Calculate its relative atomic mass to 3 significant figures.
practice.a: (63 × 69.5) + (65 × 30.5) = 6361 1; ÷ 100 = 63.61 1; = 63.6 1.

practice.q: State what is meant by isotopes.
practice.a: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons 1; but different numbers of neutrons 1.

bands.title: The skills that decide your grade
bands.note: Not topics — habits. These cost marks across every question on every paper.

items.claim: Graph craft: sharp pencil, one smooth line, construction lines left on
items.why: Marks are awarded for the working lines themselves, and lost for feathery or sketchy best-fit curves. Read the curve the question actually names.

mustKnow.gist: SHARP PENCIL. PLOT WITHIN HALF A SQUARE. CLEAR × OR DOT.
mustKnow.exact: Sharp pencil. Plot to the nearest gridline, within half a square, with a clear × or dot.

mustKnow.gist: ONE SMOOTH BEST-FIT LINE. NOT FURRY, NOT SKETCHY, NOT BLUNT PENCIL.
mustKnow.exact: ONE single smooth best-fit line. 2023 penalised "blunt pencils, sketchy/feathery lines instead of a single one".

mustKnow.gist: LINE MISS SOME POINT? FINE — BUT SAME NUMBER OF POINT EACH SIDE.
mustKnow.exact: If the line does not pass through every point, the points must be EVENLY DISTRIBUTED either side.

mustKnow.gist: START AT ZERO ONLY IF DATA SAY SO. IF IT DO, START THERE CLEARLY.
mustKnow.exact: Start at the origin only when the data says so — but when it does, start there CLEARLY.

mustKnow.gist: IGNORE THE ODD POINT WHEN DRAWING LINE, BUT LEAVE IT PLOTTED.
mustKnow.exact: Ignore an anomaly when drawing the line, but leave it plotted.

mustKnow.gist: ALWAYS LEAVE YOUR READING LINES ON THE GRAPH. THEY ARE MARKS.
mustKnow.exact: Always leave your construction lines on the graph for any value read off — worth marks in themselves.

mustKnow.gist: LABEL BOTH AXIS WITH THING AND UNIT. LABEL EACH CURVE IF MORE THAN ONE.
mustKnow.exact: Label both axes with the QUANTITY and the UNIT, and label each curve when there is more than one.

mustKnow.gist: READ THE CURVE THEY NAME.
mustKnow.exact: Read the curve the question names.

practice.q: You read the right value off a solubility graph but score 1 of 2. Why?
practice.a: The construction lines were not shown on the graph — the working line is a mark in its own right 1.

items.claim: Say which species, not just what happened
items.why: "The magnesium ION gains electrons", "iron(III) OXIDE is reduced", "the bromide IONS lose electrons". Naming the wrong species is the single most penalised error in the whole five years.

mustKnow.gist: AT ELECTRODE IT IS THE ION: "MAGNESIUM ION GAIN ELECTRON", "BROMIDE ION LOSE ELECTRON".
mustKnow.exact: At an electrode it is the ION that gains or loses electrons: "the magnesium ION gains electrons", "the bromide IONS lose electrons".

mustKnow.gist: IN REDOX, NAME THE WHOLE COMPOUND: "IRON(III) OXIDE REDUCED", "OXYGEN REMOVED FROM CALCIUM PHOSPHATE".
mustKnow.exact: In redox by oxygen, name the WHOLE compound: "iron(III) OXIDE is reduced", "oxygen is removed from calcium PHOSPHATE".

mustKnow.gist: CONDUCTING: SAY WHAT MOVE. ION FOR IONIC, ELECTRON FOR METAL AND GRAPHITE. MIX THEM = ZERO.
mustKnow.exact: For conduction, name the moving particle: IONS for ionic compounds, ELECTRONS for metals and graphite. Mixing them scores zero.

mustKnow.gist: OH⁻ IN SOLUTION COME FROM WATER SPLITTING. NOT "BECAUSE IT ALKALINE".
mustKnow.exact: OH⁻ ions in a solution come from water dissociating — not "because the solution is alkaline".

mustKnow.gist: NAMING THE EXACT THING = THE MOST PUNISHED MISTAKE IN ALL FIVE YEAR.
mustKnow.exact: This one habit — naming the exact species — is the most heavily penalised error across all five years.

practice.q: A student writes "magnesium gains electrons at the cathode". Correct it and explain what is wrong.
practice.a: It should read "the magnesium ION gains electrons" 1; before the electrons arrive there is no magnesium metal, only an Mg²⁺ ion, which BECOMES magnesium: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg 1.

items.claim: Obey the answer line: units, significant figures, standard form
items.why: Whole marks exist purely for writing the answer in standard form or to the stated number of significant figures.

mustKnow.gist: READ THE ANSWER LINE BEFORE YOU START. IT NAME THE UNIT, OFTEN THE SIG FIG TOO.
mustKnow.exact: Read the answer line BEFORE calculating: it names the unit, and often the significant figures or standard form.

mustKnow.gist: WHOLE MARK JUST FOR STANDARD FORM, OR FOR OBEYING "2 SIGNIFICANT FIGURES".
mustKnow.exact: Whole marks exist purely for standard form (4.8 × 10⁶) or for obeying "give your answer to 2 significant figures".

mustKnow.gist: BIG AND TINY NUMBER STAY STANDARD FORM: 2.4 × 10²².
mustKnow.exact: Large and small numbers stay in standard form — 2.4 × 10²², not the digits written out.

mustKnow.gist: ROUND AT THE END ONLY.
mustKnow.exact: Round only at the END of a calculation.

mustKnow.gist: UNIT MATTER: cm³ NOT cm, min NOT m. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
mustKnow.exact: Units are chemistry: cm³ not cm, min not m, and 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

mustKnow.gist: MATCH MOLAR VOLUME TO THE UNIT THEY WANT: 24 dm³ OR 24 000 cm³.
mustKnow.exact: Match the molar volume to the unit demanded: 24 dm³ or 24 000 cm³.

practice.q: 0.0405 mol of H₂ is produced. Calculate the number of molecules, to 2 significant figures. [1 mol = 6.0 × 10²³]
practice.a: 0.0405 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 2.43 × 10²² 1; = 2.4 × 10²² 1.

items.claim: Observations are what you SEE
items.why: Effervescence, a blue precipitate, the ribbon disappearing. Naming a gas is a conclusion and scores nothing as an observation.

mustKnow.gist: OBSERVATION = YOU CAN SEE IT: BUBBLES · BLUE SOLID APPEAR · COLOUR GO · RIBBON DISAPPEAR.
mustKnow.exact: An observation is visible: effervescence/bubbles · a blue precipitate forms · the solution goes colourless · the ribbon disappears.

mustKnow.gist: NAMING A GAS OR PRODUCT IS A CONCLUSION. SCHEME IGNORE IT.
mustKnow.exact: Naming a gas or a product is a CONCLUSION, not an observation — the schemes ignore it.

mustKnow.gist: DO NOT ADD EXTRA WRONG STUFF. "WHITE FLAME" GOT REJECTED.
mustKnow.exact: Do not decorate with extra wrong observations: 2021 rejected answers that added "white flame".

mustKnow.gist: PRECIPITATION MAKE NO GAS, SO "FIZZING" IS WRONG THERE.
mustKnow.exact: Precipitation reactions make NO gas, so "fizzing" is wrong there — 2023 rejected it.

mustKnow.gist: IF THEY TELL YOU A SOLID FORMED, SAY WHAT IT LOOK LIKE. DO NOT JUST REPEAT IT FORMED.
mustKnow.exact: Read the question: if it tells you a precipitate formed, describe what it LOOKS like, do not just repeat that one formed.

practice.q: Copper(II) sulfate solution is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution. State what you would see.
practice.a: A blue precipitate/solid forms, and the blue solution fades 1. Fizzing is wrong — no gas is produced.

practice.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute acid. Give two observations.
practice.a: Effervescence/bubbles 1; the ribbon disappears/gets smaller 1. "Hydrogen is given off" is a conclusion.
